source.title_on_document: Generative AI Enhances Team Performance and Reduces Need for Traditional Teams

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials on OSF: https://osf.io/zq48w/?view_only=ca644891d4234935b1464fbc20ce6e85 (p. 8, footnote 3). Preregistration: https://osf.io/5su8c/?view_only=24f9efec395c4581b880e7773792d23d (p. 4, footnote 1).
supplement.holds: Lab setting, task details, rating scales for judges, post-experiment questionnaire, and the method for the GPT-4 'human input' indicator (pp. 8, 10, 19). All regression tables and arm means/SDs are in Appendices A and B of this PDF, so no outcome statistics appear to sit only in the supplement.

paper_design_summary: Experiment I: 435 working professionals and college students in a behavioral lab were randomly allocated to 122 teams of three to five, and teams were randomly assigned to human-only, single-AI (one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint per team), or multiple-AI (one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint per member) conditions; each team completed an article-writing task and a digital-transformation strategy task. An online panel of six blind judges rated each output 1 to 10 on overall quality, novelty, and usefulness. Experiment II: 139 separately recruited individuals each worked alone with ChatGPT 4.0 on the same two tasks, and their rated outputs were compared with the Experiment I teams (no random assignment between individuals and teams).

studies.label: Experiment I (teams: human-only vs single-AI vs multiple-AI)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were randomly allocated to teams; teams were randomly assigned to human-only, single-AI (one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint), or multiple-AI (one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint per member) conditions.

arms.name: Human-only team
arms.description: Teams worked without AI. After submission they received one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint to refine outputs, but the paper excludes that refinement from analysis (p. 9, footnote 4). 42 teams, 84 task outputs.

arms.name: Single-AI team
arms.description: Team given one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint. 41 teams, 82 task outputs.

arms.name: Multiple-AI team
arms.description: Team given as many ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoints as members. 39 teams, 78 task outputs.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper gives people per arm only at assignment (142/150/143, p. 9; Figure 1 note p. 26). Table 1 (p. 34) shows all 122 teams (42/41/39) and 244 team-task outputs (84/82/78) in the analysis, so n_analyzed = 435 is the assigned count with no stated exclusions; the paper never states a people count after exclusions. Analysis unit is the team-task output (N = 244). Task completion time regressions use N = 235 outputs (Table 7, p. 43).
participants.who: Working professionals in marketing, operations, technology research, and general management, plus college students; mean team age 25.774 (Appendix A, p. 34).
participants.country: not_stated (authors at Tsinghua University; country of the lab not stated)
participants.quote: The study drew on a diverse cohort of 435 working professionals spanning various industries such as marketing, operations, technology research, and general management, in addition to college students.

ai_tool.how_used: Teams used ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoints freely while producing the outputs; chat logs were extracted for mechanism analysis (p. 10). Single-AI: one touchpoint shared by the team; multiple-AI: one per member.

task.description: Two professional tasks per team: (1) a content-generation task writing a series of in-depth articles on college students' job hunting and career development; (2) a strategy-development task designing a digital transformation strategy for a traditional retail chain (p. 9). Analyses pool both tasks with task fixed effects. Closest single codes: creative_writing (Task 1) and idea_generation (Task 2).
task.duration: not_stated (completion time analyzed in log units, Table 7, but no time limit stated)

outcomes.name: Overall quality (judge rating, 1-10)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Online panel of judges, blind to hypotheses and conditions; six independent raters per output; 1-10 scale following Amabile (1983); Cronbach's alpha 0.759 (p. 10). Coded usefulness because the codebook lists 'quality' there; could be read as overall_creativity (see open_questions). OLS on team-task outputs with task fixed effects and standardized team controls (age, gender, education, IQ, AI use, size, familiarity); robust (not team-clustered) SEs. Per-task means in Table 1 (p. 34). Robustness: relative-distribution plots (Figure 5, p. 30).

studies.label: Experiment II (individuals working alone with ChatGPT 4.0, compared with Experiment I teams)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not assigned. 139 participants were recruited separately to the lab and all worked alone with ChatGPT 4.0; their outputs were pooled with the Experiment I teams and compared by OLS. The paper calls it a 'post-hoc study' (p. 21).
assignment.quote: We enlisted a diverse cohort of 139 participants to our behavior lab. ... Each participant then individually worked with ChatGPT4.0 to complete the two tasks.
assignment.prereg_locator: The preregistration (p. 4, footnote 1) is described for the three-condition team experiment; nothing says Experiment II was preregistered.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No other paper named. Within the paper, Experiment II re-uses the Experiment I teams (435 people, 122 teams) as comparison groups.
sample_overlap.quote: we employed OLS regression on a dataset that included 139 individuals from Experiment II and 122 teams from Experiment I

company_involvement.description: Funded by Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management Research Grant (No. 2022051001) and Tsinghua University Research Grant (No. 2023THZWJC01); no company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: Experiment I (S1) randomly assigned 122 teams (435 people) to human-only, single-AI, or multiple-AI ChatGPT 4.0 conditions (p. 9), well above 50 people, and blind online judges rated each team output on overall quality, novelty, and usefulness (p. 10). Assignment is clustered at the team level and the analysis unit is the team-task output (N = 244) with robust, not team-clustered, SEs. Experiment II (S2) is a non-randomized comparison of 139 individuals working with AI against the Experiment I teams and is context only (quasi_people).

one_line_finding: In a lab experiment with 435 people in 122 randomly assigned teams, AI-assisted teams scored higher than human-only teams on judge-rated overall quality (0.417, SE 0.148), novelty (0.344, SE 0.150), and usefulness (0.250, SE 0.150) on a 1-10 scale, with no difference between single- and multiple-AI teams (Appendix B Tables 1-4, pp. 37-40).
open_questions: Construct for 'overall quality': coded usefulness because the codebook lists 'quality' under usefulness; it is the paper's headline measure and Review could treat it as overall_creativity.

Task type: two tasks (article writing and business strategy) are pooled in every regression; coded 'other'. Per-task arm means and SDs exist in Appendix A Table 1 (p. 34) if separate creative_writing and idea_generation records are wanted.

Unit and SEs: outcomes are at the team-task output level (two outputs per team) with robust SEs, not clustered by team, and randomization is by team; participant-level SD is not defined because outputs are team products.

Text vs table discrepancy for the Bayesian multiple- vs single-AI estimates: p. 13 prints Overall -0.072 [-0.303, 0.169], Novelty 0.025 [-0.220, 0.262], Usefulness 0.076 [-0.184, 0.323]; Appendix B Table 4 (p. 40) prints -0.024 [-0.273, 0.200], 0.094 [-0.170, 0.367], 0.065 [-0.154, 0.296]. The form records both.
p. 18 text reports AI-team novelty in Table 9 as 'beta = 0.372, p > .05' while Table 9 (p. 45) shows 0.372** (0.147).
Arm-level people counts after analysis are not printed; n_analyzed equals the assigned counts because Table 1 includes all 122 teams.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output or answer none of the three questions: task completion time (Tables 7-8, pp. 43-44), self-reported team processes (coordination, potency, information elaboration, satisfaction; Tables 16-17, pp. 52-53; AI teams higher on potency 0.313** and satisfaction 0.266*), heterogeneity by team IQ/size/familiarity (Table 5, p. 41), and mechanism analyses of prompt length, interaction rounds, GPT-4-scored human input, and Gini of contributions (Tables 13-15, pp. 49-51). Footnote 4 (p. 9): human-only teams got one ChatGPT 4.0 touchpoint after submitting, and that refinement is excluded from analysis. No diversity (across_people) or after_ai outcomes are reported.
